Modern Java has dramatically transformed how we inspect object types and branch through control flow statements via Pattern Matching for instanceof and switch. Historically, Java developers suffered from heavy boilerplate when handling polymorphic hierarchies. Checking if an object was an instance of a specific type required an explicit type check followed immediately by a redundant downcasting operation, increasing cognitive load and introducing opportunities for ClassCastException if refactored carelessly. Pattern Matching for instanceof eliminates this by introducing 'pattern variables'—temporary bindings that automatically cast the target object when the type check succeeds. This shifts code away from defensive boilerplate toward declarative type safety.

Building upon this foundation, Pattern Matching for switch elevates the classic switch statement from a primitive jump-table over integers and enums into a powerful expression-matching engine. Combined with sealed classes, switch patterns enable exhaustive type checking at compile time. The compiler ensures every possible subclass of a sealed hierarchy is handled, eliminating the dangerous default clauses that masked missing cases during domain evolution. Furthermore, guard patterns (using the when keyword) allow developers to combine structural type matching with boolean conditional filtering within a single case label, bridging the gap between algebraic data types and imperative execution.

rows: Requires manual instanceof check followed by explicit cast
Automatic binding via pattern variables (flow scoping)
Limited to primitive constants, Strings, and enums
Supports arbitrary reference types, null checks, and type patterns
Cannot enforce compile-time exhaustiveness over types
Enforces total coverage when matching against sealed hierarchies
Requires nested if statements inside switch blocks
Supports refined filtering via guard patterns (when expressions)

items: Flow scoping relies on definite assignment rules: a pattern variable is only in scope where the compiler can mathematically guarantee the match succeeded, such as the true branch of an if statement.
Type patterns in switch statements support total type matching as well as conditional refinement using the 'when' guard keyword without altering the dominant order of case labels.
Null-hostility in legacy switch is partially addressed: modern switch statements can explicitly handle null references using case null, preventing unexpected NullPointerException crashes.
Deconstruction patterns (enhanced via JEP 440/441/444) extend this paradigm to record classes, allowing developers to unpack component states directly inside the pattern match expression.

parsed_answer.content: Beware of dominant case ordering when writing switch patterns. The Java compiler enforces that more specific patterns must appear before broader patterns (e.g., matching a subtype before its sealed supertype). Placing a raw type pattern or a broader interface match above a specific record or subtype pattern will trigger a compile-time error regarding unreachable code. Additionally, remember that flow-scoped pattern variables are mutable if declared without final, though mutating pattern variables inside a conditional block is considered an anti-pattern.

title: (Java 17+) Pattern Matching for instanceof and switch.
